case_name: Canadian Jewish Congress v. Board of School Trustees, District No. 15
text:
REVISED HEADING

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL
OF NEW BRUNSWICK

Stratton, C.J.N.B., Hoyt and Ryan,
JJ.A

Date: 19890908

Dockets: 31/89/CA; 36/89/CA;
37/89/CA

BETWEEN:

CANADIAN JEWISH CONGRESS

INTERVENOR / APPELLANT

-and-

THE MINISTER OF LABOUR

(Respondent)                                     APPELLANT

DISTRICT NO. 15 and THE NEW BRUNSWICK TEACHERS' FEDERATION

(Applicants)                                       RESPONDENTS

-and-

ATTIS, HUMAN RIGHTS COMMISSION, DEPARTMENT OF EDUCATION, MALCOLM ROSS and BRIAN
D. BRUCE

FEDERATION

(Applicant)                                         RESPONDENT

AND BETWEEN:

CANADIAN JEWISH CONGRESS

INTERVENOR / APPELLANT

-and-

DAVID ATTIS

(Respondent)                                     APPELLANT

-and-

THE BOARD OF SCHOOL TRUSTEES,
DISTRICT NO. 15

(Applicant)                                         RESPONDENT

[Page
3]

DATE OF HEARING:                                               May
23, 1989

DATE OF DECISION:                                              September
8, 1989

REASONS FOR JUDGMENT BY:                          Stratton,
C.J.N.B.

CONCURRED IN BY:                                               Hoyt,
J.A.

REASONS DISSENTING IN PART BY:                 Ryan, J.A.

COUNSEL

Neil Finkelstein, Esq. for Canadian
Jewish Congress

Gabriel Bourgeois, Esq. for The Minister of Labour

James C. Letcher. Q.C. for The Board of School Trustees,
District No.15.

E. J. Mockler, Q.C. and Patrick Hurley, Esq. for The New
Brunswick Teachers’ Federation

No one appeared for Human Rights Board of Inquiry,
Department of Education or Brian D. Bruce.

Joseph E. Weir, Esq. for David Attis.

Joanne E. McLeod, Esqe. and Thomas S. Kuttner, Esq. for
Human Rights Commission.

Malcom Ross appeared in person.

BY THE COURT

The
appeals are allowed. The order purporting to quash the order of the Minister of
Labour is set aside, thereby permitting the Board of Inquiry to proceed.

STRATTON,
C.J.N.B.

There
are essentially four issues raised by these three appeals:
(1)
Is judicial review available to
prohibit a Board of Inquiry established under the
Human Rights Act
,

R.S.N.B. 1973, c.H-11, from proceeding with a hearing;
(2)
the interpretation to be given the
Human Rights Act

and, in particular, whether public education is
governed by subsection 5(1) thereof;
(3)
the status of David Attis as a grievor under the Act;
and
(4)

whether Mr. Attis' written complaint to the New
Brunswick Human Rights Commission was sufficiently precise to constitute a
valid complaint.

THE FACTUAL BACKGROUND

On
or about April 21, 1988, by a statement in writing on a form provided by and
filed with the New Brunswick Human Rights Commission, the appellant David Attis
complained against the respondent the Board of School Trustees of District No.
15. The complaint alleged discrimination under s.5 of the
Human Rights Act

during the period March 29, 1977 to April 21, 1988.

Mr.
Attis is a member of the Jewish community. Three of his children are enrolled
as students in School District No. 15. He claims that by its statements and its
inaction the School Board has condoned what he perceives to be the anti-semitic
and discriminatory views of Malcolm Ross, a teacher employed in School District
15. Mr. Attis alleges that Mr. Ross has publicized these views by making
racist, discriminatory and bigoted statements to his students during the
1976-77 school year, through his

[Page
2]

writings in at least two
books, and by widely published newspaper statements. Mr. Attis contends that
the School Board has provided a racist and anti-Jewish role model for its
students, has fostered a climate where students are at ease expressing
anti-Jewish views, and has reduced the credibility of its official history
curriculum, thus depriving Jewish and other minority students of equality of
opportunity with respect to a public service.

In
his written statement Mr. Attis said:

I am a
Jew and three of my children are enrolled as students within District #15.

I have reason to
believe that Malcolm Ross, a teacher employed by the School Board, made racist,
discriminatory and bigoted statements to his students during the 1976-77 school
year. I have reason to believe that the School Board knew of this, yet it
merely transferred Malcolm Ross to another school.

Malcolm Ross has
written at least two books (i.e. Web of Deceit and Spectre of Power) and has
made widely published statements (e.g. Miramichi Leader, October 22, 1986, page
5) that are anti-Jewish, racist, bigoted and discriminatory and that deny that
six

million Jews died during the Nazi Holocaust.

On April 22, 1987,
the School Board failed to pass a motion condemning bigotry and racism. On
March 15 or 16, 1988, Ray Maybee, a member of the School Board, publicly stated
that Malcolm Ross' opinions were well documented and he had done his homework,
thus appearing

[Page
3]

to support Mr. Ross' discriminatory views.
Furthermore, when the School Board reprimanded Malcolm Ross on March 15, 1988,
it referred to his views merely as controversial rather than discriminatory and
the reprimand applied only to his future actions, not his past actions.

By its
own statements and its inaction over Malcolm Ross' statements in class and in
public, the School Board has condoned his views, has thus provided a racist and
anti-Jewish role model for its students, has fostered a climate where students
feel more at ease expressing anti-Jewish views, and has reduced the credibility
of the content of its official history curriculum, thus depriving Jews and
other minority students of equal opportunity within the educational system that
the School Board provides as a service to the public.

I
believe that the School Board has thus furthered the aims of the Ross' of our
society. I would like to give a couple of examples:

i)

Several
students at the Magnetic Hill School intend to present a petition to the
Premier of New Brunswick in support of Malcolm Ross. When asked if they
concurred with Ross' views, the students replied that they didn't know.

ii)

My
eldest daughter, a grade 6 student at Beaverbrook School was invited by a
friend to attend a gymnastic exhibition at Magnetic Hill School. She was
reminded by a classmate that she shouldn't go there because that is "where
the teacher who hates Jews" works. She attended nevertheless.

[Page
4]

I have reasonable cause to believe that the Board of
School Trustees of District #15 has violated Section 5 of the Human Rights Act.

Upon
receipt of Mr. Attis' written statement the Human Rights Commission, through a
human rights officer, inquired into his allegations as required by section 18
of the
Human Rights Act

and
attempted to effect a settlement of the matter. However, no settlement was
reached. On September 1, 1988 the Commission recommended to the provincial
Minister of Labour that a Board of Inquiry be appointed to investigate the
matter as provided by section 20 of the
Act
.
On that same day, the Minister appointed Professor
Brian D. Bruce of the Faculty of Law at the University of New Brunswick as the
Board of Inquiry.

The
Board of Inquiry was scheduled to hold its first hearing on November 21, 1988.
On November 17, 1988 Mr. Justice Miller of the Court of Queen's Bench ordered a
stay of proceedings by the Board of Inquiry pending the final disposition of
two applications for judicial review filed by the School Board and the New
Brunswick Teachers' Federation seeking to prohibit the Board from proceeding
with its inquiry.

THE DECISION APPEALED FROM

In
a decision dated January 19, 1989 Mr. Justice Miller granted the applications
for judicial

[Page
5]

review and quashed the
order of the Minister of Labour which had established the Board of Inquiry. In
the course of his reasons for decision, Miller, J. made three pivotal rulings.
First, he held that in appropriate circumstances a court has the power to order
that an established administrative tribunal be prohibited from acting. He
observed, however, that this power is to be exercised with extreme caution;
but, he said, if an applicant can properly raise an issue of law then the
applicant can seek a prohibition order by way of judicial review prior to the
tribunal undertaking its inquiry. Second, he held that the provision of school
facilities and an education program are not included within the meaning of
"accommodation, services and facilities" as found in section 5 of the

Human
Rights Act
.
Third, the Judge of first instance
held that the allegations in the written statement filed by Mr.
Attis
were not specific enough to qualify as a complaint within
the meaning of the
Act
.

He pointed out that the Board of Inquiry must not only know what it is
being asked to consider, but the School Board against whom the complaint is
made must know what allegations it faces. He added too that a representative
claim is not envisaged by the
Act
. The legislation, he said, can only be set in motion
by a proper complaint from an aggrieved party alleging discrimination within
the provisions of the statute.

From
the decision of Miller, J. three separate appeals were filed in this Court. But
all three appeals involve the same issues and were consolidated and heard on
the same date. In my opinion, only one decision is necessary to dispose of all
three appeals.

[Page
6]

THE ARGUMENTS

The
Minister of Labour, Mr. David Attis, the Human Rights Commission and the
Canadian Jewish Congress submit that Miller, J. erred by usurping the Board of
Inquiry's statutorily assigned rights and duties to hear and adjudicate upon the
matter. These parties further contend that the judge misinterpreted section 5
of the
Human Rights Act

as
not including educational services rendered by the New Brunswick public school
system and incorrectly held that the complaint was too imprecise and that Mr.
Attis was not a person aggrieved under the
Act
. They further contend that the
trial Judge's findings of fact were too extensive based only on affidavit
evidence on an application for judicial review, and the quashing of the
Minister's order was incorrect since the Minister had exercised an
administrative function that could not be the subject of a judicial review
order of that nature. Finally, David Attis argues that the New Brunswick
Teachers' Federation lost any right it may have had to request a judicial
review order by seeking participation in the formal hearing of the Board of
Inquiry.

On
the other hand, the Board of School Trustees, the New Brunswick Teachers'
Federation and Malcolm Ross submit that if the complaint is not a proper complaint
then that decision is a question of law that does not depend upon the finding
of certain facts. Further, they submit, Miller, J. was correct in construing
section 5 of the
Human Rights Act
as not including educational services rendered by the
public school system; in holding that the complaint of David Attis does not
describe a discriminatory situation;

[Page
7]

and in deciding that Mr.
Attis was not the object of personal discrimination and was purporting to speak
on behalf of a group. Moreover, the New Brunswick Teachers' Federation submits
that it has standing to question the jurisdiction of the Board of Inquiry on
judicial review as a party to the inquiry.

DISCUSSION

I.

Introduction

I
think it is of singular importance at the outset of these reasons to state what
the Court is called upon to decide in these three appeals and, of equal
importance, what it is not called upon to decide. It has been asked to decide
the availability of judicial review, the interpretation of section 5 of the
Human Rights Act,

the status of David Attis as a complainant and the
sufficiency of the complaint. It has not been called upon to decide, or even to
enter, the clamorous and continuing public debate concerning the published
writings and public statements of Malcolm Ross.

II.

Availability of Judicial Review

An
application for judicial review to prohibit an administrative tribunal from
proceeding may be sought as soon as an absence of jurisdiction has either

[Page
8]

arisen or may clearly be
foreseen. The main advantage of such an application is that it may be brought
to test the validity of proceedings before they are undertaken with a possible
saving of time and expense. However, an application for judicial review to
prevent an apprehended error of law may be premature where the tribunal has not
yet had a chance to find facts on which its jurisdiction depends; see
Reid and David,
Administrative Law and Practice
,

(2nd
edition, 1978,) pp.340-341. The guiding principle would seem to be that where
there is a clear question of law not depending upon particular facts, there is
no reason why an applicant should not go directly to the Court for a judicial
review order prohibiting a tribunal from proceeding rather than waiting to see
if the decision goes against him, in which case he would then have to move to
quash the decision: see
Regina v. Tottenham and District Rent Tribunal
,

[1957] 1 Q.B. 103
, per Lord Goddard, C.J., at p.108.

The
decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in
Bell v. Ontario Human Rights Commission,

1971 CanLII 195 (SCC)
,
[1971] S.C.R. 756
was relied upon by the Judge of first
instance as authority for the granting
of
an
order of prohibition in the circumstances of the present case.
In
Bell
,

the majority of the Court held that prohibition was
available to prevent proceedings investigating a complaint under the
Ontario Human
Rights Code

involving a question of law. Mr.
Justice Martland, speaking for the majority, described the inter-relationship
between facts and law for such an application at pp.774-775:

[Page
9]

The
present case raises a question of law as to the meaning of the phrase
"self-contained dwelling unit." The facts involved in relation to
whether or not the appellant's premises available for rent were within that
phrase relate only to the structure of a building and
do not involve
choosing between the conflicting testimony of witnesses. In a case involving a
conflict of evidence a Court to which an application for prohibition was made
might well decline to interfere.

…

The powers given to a board of inquiry are to enable it to
determine whether or not there has been discrimination in respect of matters
within the scope of the Act. It has no power to deal with alleged
discrimination in matters not within the purview of the Act or to make
recommendations with respect thereto.

…

In my opinion
the appellant was
not compelled to await the decision of the board on that issue before seeking
to have it determined in a court of law by an application for prohibition and
the Court had jurisdiction to deal with the matter
.

(Emphasis
added)

In
a subsequent decision,
Re
CIP
Paper Products Ltd.
and Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission

(1978),
1978 CanLII 1847 (SK CA)
,
87 D.L.R. (3d) 609
, Chief Justice Culliton,
speaking for the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, attempted to limit the application
of the
Bell

decision.
He wrote at p.612:

Care
must be taken not to give to the decision in
Bell v. Ontario
Human

[Page
10]

Rights
Commission

too wide an application.
That case simply decided that, where
there is a clear point of law not depending upon particular facts upon the
determination of which the jurisdiction of the tribunal depends, that
determination may be made in an application for prohibition
.
That judgment did
not decide that prohibition lies on the contention that the complaint is one which
cannot be sustained within the provisions of the Act in respect to which the
complaint is made. The decision as to whether the complaint is one which is
contemplated by the pertinent legislation, and, if so, whether discrimination
is, or is not, established, are matters for the Human Rights Commission. Such
statutory rights and duties of the Commission cannot be usurped by the Court
under the guise of prohibition proceedings in which is sought, in effect, a
determination of the complaint on its merits.

(Emphasis
added)

It
is perhaps trite to note that there are numerous authoritative decisions which
have directed courts to exercise restraint and curial deference when dealing
with the specialized jurisdiction confided to statutory tribunals. It has been
said that a court ought not to preempt a statutory tribunal nor usurp its
rights and duties under the guise of prohibition proceedings. Nor should a
court be astute to hold that Parliament did not intend the tribunal to have
jurisdiction to decide for itself the meaning of ordinary words used in the
statute to define the question which it has to decide. On the other hand, it
has

[Page
11]

also been said that it
is a jurisdictional error for a human rights commission to set up an inquiry
when the subject matter of the inquiry cannot involve a contravention of the
Act: see
Re Alberta Human Rights Commission and The Queen

(1986),
1986 ABCA 32 (CanLII)
,
27 D.L.R. (4th) 735 (Alberta C.A.)
at p.736
.

The

non-interventionist

approach to judicial review of
administrative bodies enunciated by the courts was recently considered by Madam
Justice L'Heureux-Dubé, dissenting, in
Tele-Communication Workers Union v.
British Columbia Telephone Company,

1988 CanLII 14 (SCC)
,
[1988] 2 S.C.R. 564
. She said at p.593:

The
deferential approach is not a licence to refuse review. It is merely a caution
to courts to recognize the proper role and function of administrative bodies.
When such bodies fail to act within jurisdiction, the Court does not have the
discretion
to intervene, it
has a
duty
to intervene at the behest of one or another of the
parties.

(Emphasis
in original)

Turning
now to the present case, it is my opinion that the three major grounds of
appeal, namely, the interpretation of section 5 of the
Human Rights Act,

the status of Mr. Attis as a complainant under the
Act

and the sufficiency of the complaint as measured
against the statutory requirements of the
Act

are questions of law that do not
concern

the determination of facts upon
which the jurisdiction of the Board of Inquiry depends. Although it could
perhaps be argued that the latter two grounds of appeal involve contested
facts, it is my opinion that the

[Page
12]

Court can restrict
itself to the questions of law dependent upon the uncontested facts adduced by
affidavit evidence.

I
am satisfied that the judge in the present case did not, either directly or
indirectly, attempt to decide the merits of the Attis complaint. Rather, he
concluded there were clear questions of law to be decided, particularly the
meaning of the phrase "accommodation, services and facilities"
contained in s.5 of the
Human Rights Act
.

While it is clear that "the Courts should not be
alert to brand as jurisdictional, and therefore subject to broader curial
review, that which may be doubtfully so" (per Dickson, J. in
C.U.P.E. Local 963
v. N. B. Liquor Corporation
,

1979 CanLII 23 (SCC)
,
[1979] 2 S.C.R. 227
at p.233)
, I am not persuaded that the Judge, who exercised
his discretion in favour of granting an order of prohibition in this instance,
did so for any improper reason.

As
previously noted, Mr. David Attis has also challenged the status of the. New
Brunswick Teachers' Federation to apply for judicial review to prohibit the
Board of Inquiry from proceeding. Mr. Attis argues that by seeking to
participate in, the inquiry as a party, the Federation acquiesced in the
Board's jurisdiction and could not subsequently challenge that jurisdiction by
means of judicial review. With respect, I can find no merit in this argument.
Acquiescence means participation in proceedings without taking objection to the
jurisdiction of the tribunal once the facts for raising the objection are fully
known: see
de Smith's Judicial Review of Administrative Action,

(4th edition, 1980) at p.423.

[Page
13]

In
the present case the Teachers' Federation sought status as a party at the
inquiry prior to the Board convening its first hearing. At the earliest
opportunity it then made an application for judicial review based on the
jurisdictional issue. I see no parallel between the present appeals and
Re Colonial Coach
Lines Ltd. et al. and Ontario Highway Transport Board et al
.

(1967),
1967 CanLII 185 (ON CA)
,
63 D.L.R. (2d) 198, (Ont.
C.A.)
.
In that case,
the hearings were well in progress when the applicant pressed the Board to make
a decision on jurisdiction. Before the Board could decide the matter, the
applicant served notice of prohibition proceedings. In my view, there is no
similar high-handed conduct by the Teachers' Federation in its application that
could be relevant in determining whether an order of prohibition should lie.

Having
concluded that this is a case which lent itself to judicial review, I turn now
to a consideration of the remaining issues, namely, the scope of s.5 of the
Human Rights Act
,
the status of a Mr. Attis as a complainant and the sufficiency
of the complaint.

III.
Interpretation
of Section 5 of Human Rights Act

A
pivotal question in the present case is whether subsection 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act

includes education in the New Brunswick public school
system.
Subsection 5(1)
of the
Human Rights Act
,

R.S.N.B.
1973
,
c.H-11 stated:

[Page
14]

5(1)
No person, directly
or indirectly, alone or with another, by himself or by the interposition of
another, shall

(a)

deny to any person or class of persons the accommodation, services, or
facilities available in any place to which the public is customarily admitted,
or

(b)

discriminate against any person or class of persons with respect to the
accommodations, services, or facilities available in any place to which the
public is customarily admitted,

because of race, colour,
religion, national origin, ancestry, place of origin, age, marital status or
sex.

The
current subsection 5(1) as amended by
An Act To Amend The Human Rights Act,
S.N.B.
1985,
c. C-30 s.7 states:

5(1)
No person,
directly or indirectly, alone or with another, by himself or by the
interposition of another, shall

(a)

deny to any person or class of persons any accommodation, services or
facilities available to the public, or

(b)

discriminate against any person or class of persons with respect to any
accommodation, services or facilities available to the public,

[Page
15]

because
of race, colour, religion, national origin, ancestry, place of origin, age,

physical disability, mental disability,
marital status or sex.

It
will be observed that the major change which has occurred in the subsection is
that the phrase "the accommodation, services, or facilities available in
any place to which the public is customarily admitted" has been amended to
read "any accommodation, services or facilities available to the
public". It could be argued that this alteration broadens the application
of the provision.

In

Gay Alliance Toward Equality v. Vancouver Sun
,
(1979)
1979 CanLII 225 (SCC)
,
2 S.C.R. 435
the Supreme
Court of Canada was called upon to interpret s.3 of the
Human Rights Code
of British Columbia

which
prohibited discrimination with respect to "any accommodation, service or
facility customarily available to the public". Martland, J., speaking for
the majority of the Court, gave some examples of the three terms used in the
section. He said at p.455:

"Accommodation" refers to such matters as
accommodation in hotels, inns and motels. "Service" refers to such
matters as restaurants, bars, taverns, service stations, public transportation
and public utilities. "Facility" refers to such matters as public
parks and recreational facilities. These are all items "customarily
available to the public".

The
majority of the Court in the
Gay Alliance

case concluded that section 3 of the
British Columbia
Human

[Page
16]

Rights
Code
did not
purport to dictate the nature and scope of a service which must be offered to
the public. Nor do I read the judgment as holding that the examples which were
given for "accommodation", "service" and
"facility" constitute an exhaustive list.

In
the current decade, the Supreme Court of Canada has consistently adopted an
expansive interpretive approach to human rights Codes and Acts. In
Insurance
Corporation of British Columbia v. Heerspink
,

1982 CanLII 27 (SCC)
,
[1982] 2 S.C.R. 145
at p.158,
Lamer, J., characterized
a human rights code as "a fundamental law". In
Ontario Human
Rights Commission v. Simpsons-Sears Ltd.,

1985 CanLII 18 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 536
, McIntyre, J., set forth the
governing principles in the interpretation of human rights statutes as follows,
at pp.546-547:

It is
not . . . a sound approach to say that according to established rules of
construction no broader meaning can be given to the Code than the narrowest
interpretation of the words employed. The accepted rules of construction are
flexible enough to enable the Court to recognize in the construction of a human
rights code the special nature and purpose of the enactment . . ., and give it
an interpretation which will advance its broad purposes. Legislation of this
type is of a special nature, not quite constitutional but certainly more than
the ordinary -- and it is for the courts to seek out its purpose and give it
effect. The Code aims at the removal of discrimination.

[Page
17]

The
purposive approach in construing human rights statutes has been followed by the
Supreme Court of Canada in
Bhinder v. Canadian National Railway Co.,

1985 CanLII 19 (SCC)
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 561
;
Action Travail des
Femmes v. Canadian National Railway Co.,

1987 CanLII 109 (SCC)
,
[1987] 1 S.C.R. 1114
, and
Robichaud v. Canada
(Treasury Board),

1987 CanLII 73 (SCC)
,
[1987] 2
S.C.R. 84
.
In
Robichaud
,

LaForest,
J. declared at p.89:

. . . [T]he Act must be so interpreted as to advance
the broad policy considerations underlying it. That task should not be
approached in a niggardly fashion but in a manner befitting the special nature
of the legislation. . .

In

Re Winnipeg School Division No. 1 and MacArthur

(1982),
1982 CanLII 2975 (MB QB)
,
133 D.L.R. (3d) 305, (Man. Q.B.)
, a decision
relied upon by the Judge of first instance, Kroft, J. held that a public school
was not an "accommodation, service or facility" within the meaning of
the
Manitoba Human Rights Act
.

In
contrast, Shannon, J. of the Alberta Supreme Court held in
Re Schmidt and
Calgary Board of Education

(1975),

1975 CanLII 254 (AB SCTD)
,
57 D.L.R. (3d) 746
; reversed on other grounds
(1976),
1976 ALTASCAD 157 (CanLII)
,
72 D.L.R. (3d) 330, (Alta
S.C., A.D.)
; that a broad and liberal interpretation permitted public schools
to fall within a similar provision.

In

Rawala and Souza v. DeVry Institute of Technology

(1982),
1982 CanLII 4880 (ON HRT)
,
3 C.H.R.R. D/1057
, an Ontario board of inquiry
ruled that a private educational institute was a service or facility provided
in a place to which the public

[Page
18]

was customarily
admitted. This case was, however, distinguished in
Sonnenberg v.
Centre Universitaire St-Louis-Maille
t

(1988),
1987 CanLII 8588 (NB BHR)
,
9 C.H.R.R. D/5100
. In the latter decision, a
New Brunswick Board of Inquiry explained that
in the
Rawala

case the premises were found to be
public since the Institute offered its facilities to the public and advertised
while the
Centre
did not advertise or promote the use of its facilities.

Thus,
it seems clear that the question whether public or private education is
governed by human rights legislation is not yet settled. It is my opinion,
however, that the
New Brunswick Human Rights Act

is

cast in wide terms and both its
subject-matter and its stated purpose suggest that it is not to be interpreted
narrowly or restrictively: see
Re Attorney-General of Canada and Cumming
et al.

(1979),
1979 CanLII 4104 (FC)
,
103 D.L.R. (3d) 151
, per
Thurlow, C.J., at p.158. When one gives to subsection 5(1) of the
Act

a "fair, large and liberal interpretation" as
required by
section 17
of the
Interpretation Act
,
R.S.N.B. 1973,c.I-13, it would, I think, undoubtedly
bring public education within its purview. To hold otherwise would seem to me
to frustrate the legislative intent of the
Human Rights Act
and its preamble and amount to a
rejection of the broad purposive approach to the interpretation of
anti-discrimination legislation adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada. As Mr.
Justice Walter S. Tarnopolsky and William F. Pentney reasoned in their text
Discrimination and
the Law
,

(1985) at p.11-47:

The two
preceding decisions,
[
Winnipeg School Division No. 1 v. McArthur
;

[Page
19]

Rawala
and Souza v. DeVry Institute of Technology
]
, illustrate the
remarkable state of Canadian law with respect to services and facilities
customarily available to the public. In Manitoba a public school is found not
to be such a service or facility, while in Ontario a private school is brought
within the scope of the legislation. It is respectfully submitted that the
McArthur

decision is
incorrect. In support of this view one need only point out that if this
decision is correct, a public school in Manitoba would not contravene the
Human Rights Act
by refusing
entrance to Indian (or Jewish or male) children. Surely such an interpretation
was not intended by the drafters of the Act nor is it necessary in order to
ensure the effective application of the law.

As
an alternative basis for my conclusion that public education is governed by
subsection 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act
,

I would adopt the reasoning of the Saskatchewan Court
of Appeal in
Re Saskatchewan Human Rights Commission et al. and
Government of Saskatchewan Department of Social Services
(1989),
1988 CanLII 212 (SK CA)
,
52 D.L.R. (4th) 253
. In that
case, the Court held that, social assistance provided under the
Saskatchewan
Assistance Act

was a service which was offered to the public and thus was affected by the
Saskatchewan Human
Rights Code

even though there were criteria for
eligibility for assistance. Vancise, J.A., explained at p.268 that the fact
that a service is offered to the public does not mean that it must be offered
to all members of the public. The government can impose eligibility
requirements to ensure that the program or

[Page
20]

services reaches the
intended client group. The only restriction is that the government cannot
discriminate among the members of the client group on the basis of the
prohibited grounds contained in the human rights legislation. Applying the
principles enunciated in this case to the present appeals, I would hold that
public education provided under the
Schools Act
,

R.S.N.B. 1973, c.S-5, is a service available to the
public. It is a service provided to a client group, the members of which meet
the eligibility requirements specified in the
Schools Act
. Thus, on this alternative basis, I
would also conclude that public education falls within the purview of
subsection 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act
.

IV.
Status
of Complainant

In
his reasons for decision, the Judge of first instance appears to indicate that
David Attis was not an aggrieved party alleging discrimination within the
Human Rights Act
.

He held that although Mr. Attis is a member of the
Jewish community in School District 15, the affidavit evidence was that neither
he nor his children had ever had direct contact with Mr. Ross as a teacher. I
would pause here to note that a trial Judge must be careful on an application
for judicial review not to rely too heavily upon the limited facts before him
in making his decision, otherwise he risks deciding the merits of the case.

It
is argued that David Attis should be given status as a complainant because he
is a parent of children enrolled in School District 15. The authority upon
which

[Page
21]

this argument is based
is
Société des Acadiens v. Minority Language School Board

(1984),
1984 CanLII 2954 (NB CA)
,
54 N.B.R. (2d) 198, (N.B.C.A.)
; affirmed

(1986),
1986 CanLII 66 (SCC)
,
69 N.B.R. (2d) 271, (S.C.C.)
. In that matter, the Association of
Parents for Fairness in Education, formed by some forty parents, moved for
leave to appeal as an intended intervenor and requested an extension of time
within which to file a notice of appeal. This Court granted an order that the
Association be given leave to appeal as a defendant in the case. The Court was
persuaded to issue the order by the parental status of the members of the
Association, but the legal foundations for the order were the
Rules of Court
,
the
Judicature Act
,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c.J-2, and in particular
section 8(2)

thereof, and the inherent jurisdiction of the Court of Appeal. Analytically, I
find the application of this precedent to these appeals to be inappropriate
because of the distinction between status in court proceedings, and status as a
complainant under the
Human Rights Act
.

In
order to discover if Mr. Attis is a proper complainant reference must be made
to section 17 of the
Human Rights Act:

17
Any person claiming
to be aggrieved because of an alleged violation of this Act may make a
complaint in writing to the Commission in a form prescribed by the Commission.

I
agree with the submission that the phrase "any person claiming to be
aggrieved" in section 17 should be given a wide interpretation. This is
particularly so at

[Page
22]

a preliminary stage
before the Board of Inquiry has held a hearing into the facts. As
stated by
Hugessen, J.A., in
Re Singh

(1988),

1988 CanLII 5665 (FCA)
,
86 N.R. 69 (Fed. C.A.)
at p. 77
:

The question as to who is the 'victim' of an alleged
discriminatory practice is almost wholly one of fact. Human rights legislation
does not look so much to the intent of discriminatory practices as to their
effect. . . . That effect is by no means limited to the alleged 'target' of the
discrimination and it is entirely conceivable that a discriminatory practice
may have consequences which are sufficiently direct and immediate to justify
qualifying as a 'victim' thereof persons who were never within the
contemplation or intent of its author.

Mr.
Attis made a written complaint to the Commission on a form prescribed by the
Commission. The section does not refer to the person filing the complaint as an
aggrieved party, as the trial Judge stated, but as a "person claiming to
be aggrieved". The Legislature has decided that it is for the Commission
and a board of inquiry to discover if there is any merit in a claim of
discrimination. Thus, I would conclude that Mr. Attis has met the statutory
standard in
section 17
to be accorded the legal status of complainant.

The
question has also been raised whether David Attis was intending to make a
representative complaint because he alleges the School Board has deprived
"Jews and other minority students of equal opportunity within the
educational system that the School Board provides as a

[Page
23]

service to the
public". In
Lévesque and Tardif v. The Daily Gleaner
,

September 10, 1974, unreported, a New Brunswick board
of inquiry held that the two complainants could not bring a complaint on behalf
of all French New Brunswickers because of the restricted definition of
"person" contained in the
Act
.
This decision was criticized by an Ontario board of
inquiry in
Tabar and Lee v. Scott and West End Construction Limited

(1982),
1982 CanLII 4887 (ON HRT)
,
3 C.H.R.R. D/1073
. Peter A.
Cummings remarked at p.D/1076:

If
there is no means by which a class of persons may enforce their rights, such
rights would be rendered nugatory. The board in
Lévesque
,

in effect, repealed
the provisions in the New Brunswick Act that prohibited discrimination against
a class of persons.

But
this issue does not have to be decided in the present appeals since the
Minister of Labour recognizes that there are no rules applicable to the
Human Rights Act

that would permit group actions, and David Attis claims
that the major thrust and intent of his complaint is not representative, but
that the School Board has discriminated against him and his children.

V.
Sufficiency
of the Complaint

The
procedures of the Commission respecting transgressions against the
Human Rights Act

are triggered by a complaint under section 17. Miller,
J., held that the Attis complaint lacked the requisite specifity. In reaching

[Page
24]

that conclusion, he
relied upon the decision of this Court in

Mackin v. Judicial
Council (N.B.)

(1988),
1987 CanLII 138 (NB CA)
,
82 N.B.R.
(2d) 203
, as defining the necessary standard for a complaint. In that case, the
Attorney-General of New Brunswick wrote a letter of "complaint" to
the Chairman of the Judicial Council
concerning

the conduct of a Provincial Court Judge. The Judicial
Council directed that an inquiry be held "into the complaint and the
report". The majority of the Court of Appeal granted an application for
judicial review for a prohibition order because in the opinion of the majority
the Attorney-General's letter fell short of being a complaint.

It
is my opinion, however, that the requirements for a complaint under the
Provincial Court
Act
,
R.S.N.B. 1973, c.P-21, to commence
an inquiry concerning the conduct of a Provincial Court Judge are not the same
as the requirements for a complaint under the
Human Rights Act
because of the special nature and
purpose of the latter enactment. The word "complaint" as used in s.17
of the
Human Rights Act
must be given an interpretation which will advance the broad purposes
of the
Act
,
i.e. the advancement of human rights and the elimination of discrimination.

In

Canadian
Human Rights Commission
v. Bell Canada

(1981),
1981 CanLII 4292 (CHRT)
,
2 C.H.R.R. D/265
, the tribunal held that any valid complaint
under the
Canadian Human Rights Act

must contain several elements. These included
identification of the
complainant,

identification of the
victim, the time during which the alleged violation took place, the location of
the alleged violation, the nature of the discriminatory practice, the relevant
section of the Act, and an

[Page
25]

affirmation by the
complainant and/or the Commission that they have reasonable grounds to believe
that the conduct constituted a discriminatory practice which violated the Act.

The

Attis
complaint appears to me to meet the statutory
requirements of
section 17
that it be in writing and on a form prescribed by
the Commission, and that it contains most of the essential elements referred to
above. On an application for judicial review this, in my opinion, is sufficient
to classify David
Attis'
written submission to the Commission
as a complaint under the Act. If further information is required during the
proceedings before the Board of Inquiry then a demand for particulars can be
made. Pursuant to s.20(3) of the
Human Rights Act

a board of inquiry has all the powers of a conciliation
board which may determine its own procedure under
subsection 66(2)
of the
Industrial
Relations Act,

R.S.N.B. 1973, c.
I-4.

It
is perhaps unnecessary to point out that it is the function of the Board of
Inquiry and not of a reviewing court to investigate the merits of a complaint.
I would, however, repeat the remarks of Thurlow, C.J. in the
Cummings

decision that in cases like the present one, it is
usually preferable for the Court to leave the tribunal free to carry out its
mandate except when it is clear and beyond doubt that the tribunal is without
jurisdiction to deal with the matter before it. In my opinion, the present case
is not within the exception.

[Page
26]

VI.

Appropriateness of the Judicial Review Order

In
his decision, Miller, J. purported to quash the order of the Minister of Labour
which established the Board of Inquiry. In issuing the order, the Minister was
acting in an administrative capacity. Therefore, the quashing of his order was
not available as a remedy in these proceedings: see
Hawley v. Richmond
County Municipal School Board

(1982),

1982 CanLII 2943 (NS CA)
,
52 N.S.R. (2d) 127, (N.S.S.C., A.D.)
and
Mehta v. MacKinnon et al.

(1985),
1985 CanLII 3117 (NS SC)
,
67 N.S.R. (2d) 429, (N.S.C.A.)
. The order
should have been expressed as prohibiting the Board of Inquiry from proceeding.

VII.

Conclusion

In
summary, it is my opinion that this is a case in which the Judge of first
instance could properly exercise his jurisdiction in favour of granting
judicial review; that public education in New Brunswick is within the purview
of subsection 5(1) of the
Human Rights Act;

that David Attis does have status as a complainant, and
that the written submission which he filed with the Commission is a complaint
under the
Act
.

For
all of the foregoing reasons, I would allow the three appeals and set aside the
order purporting to quash the order of the Minister of Labour, thereby
permitting the Board of Inquiry to proceed. In the circumstances, I would make
no order as to cost.

Chief Justice of New Brunswick

I
CONCUR:

[S]

W. L. HOYT, J.A.

RYAN, J.A.

I
have read the reasons for judgment of Chief Justice Stratton and concur with
him except with respect to his categorization of the status of the complainant
and the sufficiency of the complaint as questions of law.

Any
person claiming to be aggrieved may file a written complaint on a form provided
by the Human Rights Commission. It seems to me that the question of who
qualifies as a "person claiming to be aggrieved" is almost wholly one
of fact, that is, a combination of fact and law. In a purist form of inquiry
both questions under review may qualify as questions of law when measured only
against the statutory requirement of the
Human Rights Act

but in this case I do not think that they ought to be
considered in such a narrow environment. As well, I believe that status and
sufficiency questions are matters which the Commission, or in this case the
board of inquiry, is well suited to answer. The Court of Queen's Bench ought
not to have intervened on these two grounds thus aborting the legislative
mandate of the Human Rights Commission, or its board, as to who is a
complainant and whether the contents of the form filed constitute a complaint.

The
main purpose of a human rights commission is to investigate complaints of
discrimination within the scope of the
Human Rights Act
.

Since this is its purpose the courts should not
goaltend access to the tribunal. On the contrary, the courts should defer to
the jurisdiction of the tribunal so that effect can be given to its purpose. I
hold this same view whether the legislative intent of the Act in question is
remedial, with punitive powers, or punitive alone.

[Page
2]

However,
I agree with the Chief Justice of New Brunswick that the judge of first instance
properly exercised his jurisdiction on judicial review on a question of law
with respect to the issue of public education, albeit the judge of first
instance came to an erroneous result in finding that the public education
system of New Brunswick is not included within the term "services"
under s.5 of the
Human Rights Act.

This erroneous decision in law, which does not concern the determination
of facts, was the proper subject of appeal for reversal by this Court. For the
reasons given by the Chief Justice with respect to the interpretation of s.5,
the appeal should be allowed.
